newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian oil output seen falling without tax reform.
newsitem.headline: Russian oil output seen falling without tax reform.

text.p: Russian oil output will go on falling and exports remain high unless Moscow makes marginal field development more economical or introduces production sharing laws, a Russian oil industry source said on Tuesday.

And if the economy picks up from its post-Soviet slump, Russia could even go short of crude, said Alexei Kocheshkov, project manager at the Association of Enterprises with Foreign Investment in Oil Production and Refining (AssoSPneft).

"Unless changes are made to the tax regime -- either through production sharing agreements or on marginal fields -- there is practically no hope of breaking the declining trend in production," he told Reuters in an interview.

Russian oil production fell to its lowest level for nearly three decades last year, totalling 293 million tonnes, or around 5.9 million barrels per day. But exports rose nine percent to 105 million tonnes (2.1 million bpd).

Russia is the world's third largest oil producer after Saudi Arabia and the United States, but it was the biggest until output declines gathered pace in the late 1980s. Production was around double current levels just 10 years ago.

"We are nearing that critical level where if the decline in output continues and the state wants to maintain high exports, then in the case of Russian gross domestic product growth, we will not have enough oil," Kocheshkov.
He said one way to reverse the decline in output was to push through legislation on production sharing which would let multi-billion-dollar deals with foreign partners go ahead.
But the legislation still faces formidable opposition in the lower house of parliament State Duma, where conservatives and nationalists are blocking its path at every step.

Kocheshkov, representing AssoSPneft, a non-governmental organisation representing joint ventures operating in Russia, said an alternative means of boosting output would be to make developing marginal fields in Russia more economical.

"In the Volga region for example, around 90 percent of remaining reserves are so-called 'difficult to recover' deposits. Under existing economic and tax issues, they are reserves that will never be developed," he said.
He said smaller independent companies involving Russia and foreign co-operation were the ideal means of ensuring that such fields were tapped.
The government needed to reduce not only excise taxes, but also royalties and mineral resource base taxation.
He said Moscow would earn more money by reducing taxes, because the volumes produced would increase dramatically.
AssoSPneft said in a recent report that joint ventures were taking a growing slice of Russian oil output and exports, although they still represented only eight and 12 percent of the country's total.
Kocheshkov said he expected the Fuel and Energy Ministry to cut down further on so-called 'state needs' exports, which go towards funding state projects, including restoring the Kremlin.
Trading companies which have dominated the exports, also known as federal programmes, are fighting a losing battle against producers, who want to control more of their own oil.
"This trend will continue," Kocheshkov said. "But some federal programmes will stay, for sure. No one would dare speak out against state needs exports being used to rebuild the Kremlin, for example."
